content: Relative volatility is a parameter that quantifies the ratio of vapor pressures between components in a liquid mixture of chemicals. It is a critical factor in the design of large-scale industrial distillation processes. Essentially, it reflects how easily or with what difficulty distillation can separate the more volatile components from the less volatile ones in a mixture. By convention, relative volatility is denoted as α (alpha). This parameter is extensively utilized in the design of various distillation processes, as well as other separation or absorption processes that involve the interaction of vapor and liquid phases across multiple equilibrium stages. However, relative volatility is not applicable in separation or absorption processes where the components chemically react with one another, such as the absorption of gaseous carbon dioxide in aqueous sodium hydroxide solutions. For a binary liquid mixture (a mixture of two components) at a specific temperature and pressure, relative volatility is defined as the ratio of the K values (vapor-liquid equilibrium constants) of the two components. When the liquid concentrations of the components are equal, the more volatile component exhibits a higher vapor pressure compared to the less volatile component. Consequently, the K value (defined as the ratio of the vapor-phase concentration to the liquid-phase concentration, y/x) for the more volatile component is larger than that of the less volatile component. This ensures that α (relative volatility) is always greater than or equal to 1, as the larger K value of the more volatile component is in the numerator, while the smaller K value of the less volatile component is in the denominator. Relative volatility is a dimensionless quantity. When the volatilities of the two key components are equal, α equals 1, making separation by distillation impossible under those conditions. As the value of α increases above 1, the separation of components by distillation becomes progressively easier. A liquid mixture containing two components is referred to as a binary mixture. When such a binary mixture undergoes distillation, complete separation of the two components is rarely achieved. Typically, the overhead fraction from the distillation column predominantly contains the more volatile component, along with a small amount of the less volatile component. Conversely, the bottoms fraction predominantly contains the less volatile component, along with a small amount of the more volatile component. In contrast, a liquid mixture containing multiple components is called a multi-component mixture. When a multi-component mixture is distilled, both the overhead and bottoms fractions generally contain more than one or two components. For instance, certain intermediate products in an oil refinery are multi-component liquid mixtures that may include alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes, ranging from methane (with one carbon atom) to decanes (with ten carbon atoms). To distill such a mixture, the distillation column may be designed to produce specific fractions. For example: An overhead fraction predominantly containing the more volatile components, such as methane (one carbon atom) to propane (three carbon atoms). A bottoms fraction predominantly containing the less volatile components, such as isobutane (four carbon atoms) to decanes (ten carbon atoms). Such a distillation column is commonly referred to as a depropanizer. In this context, the designer would designate the key components governing the separation design as propane (the so-called light key, LK) and isobutane (the so-called heavy key, HK). Here, a lighter component refers to one with a lower boiling point (or higher vapor pressure), while a heavier component refers to one with a higher boiling point (or lower vapor pressure). The values of K (vapor-liquid equilibrium constants) have been empirically or theoretically correlated in terms of temperature, pressure, and phase compositions. These correlations are often presented in the form of equations, tables, or graphs, such as the well-known DePriester charts. K values are widely employed in the design of large-scale distillation columns for separating multi-component mixtures in industries such as oil refineries, petrochemical and chemical plants, natural gas processing facilities, and other related sectors.
